story.title: The erroneous character should not dominate the search
paragraphs: Chinese Spelling Check (CSC) corrects misspelled characters, which are usually confused with characters of similar sound or shape. In CSC, part of the retrieval query is wrong: a key that encodes the mistaken character can retrieve fluent uses of that character and reinforce the error.

Strong correctors also underuse their training data: in Table 1, REALISE, a multimodal CSC model, leaves 设 (set) uncorrected where 这 (this) is meant, although that error appears in similar contexts in the training set. RERIC turns the training set into a datastore that the corrector consults at inference.

mechanism.title: Dense retrieval finds candidates; local overlap corrects their ranking
paragraphs: Each key concatenates the target character's phonetic and glyph representations from REALISE with a Gaussian-weighted average of the fused semantic, phonetic, and glyph representations of nearby tokens, so it reflects the surrounding characters rather than only the target's possibly wrong meaning. Queries are built the same way, and every training token is stored, correct or not.

Each value is the corrected 3-gram around the target. Dense retrieval alone can rank 这以后 first for the input 这以个 because it shares the wrong character 以; reranking rewards positional overlap with the input window and downweights a match at the center. The reranked distribution is interpolated with REALISE's own prediction, without retraining REALISE.

evidence.title: Much of the gain comes from avoiding unnecessary corrections
paragraphs: On SIGHAN15, the 2015 test set of the SIGHAN Chinese spelling-check shared tasks, nearly all of the gain over REALISE comes from precision (Table 4): RERIC makes fewer wrong corrections rather than finding more errors. In the case study, REALISE changes a correct 带 (take) to 戴 (wear); RERIC, with many correct uses of 带 in its datastore, does not.

The key design, not retrieval itself, carries the gain: replacing the key's context part with the token's semantic representation falls below no retrieval (Table 5). Retrieval adds about 6% inference time and a 1.3 GB datastore; adding about one million error-free Chinese Wikipedia articles to the datastore raises SIGHAN15 correction F1 from 80.0 to 80.9 without retraining (Table 7).

reading_notes: Re-read key construction, Gaussian context, weighted n-gram overlap Equation 11, mixture Equation 13, Table 3 hyperparameters, precision/recall Table 4. v5 demo uses w = (1.68, 0.68, 1.68) and n = 3 as printed; with these values α exceeds 1 when both neighbors match, so (1 − α) is negative. Distances are reader-set and labeled illustrative. The released repository contains no code to check normalization.

demo.title: Should matching the wrong character count?
demo.description: RERIC reranks retrieved 3-grams by their positional overlap with the input window: α sums the weights of the matching positions, and the retrieval distance is multiplied by 1 − α (Equation 11). By default α is divided by the sum of the weights, so that a full match gives α = 1; switch to the printed normalization (÷ n = 3) to see what the equation gives with the Table 3 weights. Move the weights and set your own distances.
demo.note: Adapted: the input window and the three candidates from Figure 1, and w = (1.68, 0.68, 1.68) with n = 3 from Table 3. Normalization: Equation 11 is printed with ÷ n; with the Table 3 weights this gives α = 1.12 when both neighbors match, so 1 − α is negative and a larger distance ranks higher. Dividing by Σw = 4.04 is our reading; it keeps α between 0 and 1 and reproduces Figure 1’s ranking with the default distances. Illustrative: the l2 distances, which the paper does not print; the defaults keep Figure 1’s retrieval order. Figure 1 lists the scores 0.93, 0.89 and 0.84 beside the candidates without defining them, so they are not used as distances. Computed: α, adjusted distances and ranks. The softmax (T = 50) and interpolation with the base model (λ = 0.4) in Equations 12–13 are not simulated. This is not a live spelling corrector.
